title: Pick your lane
teaches: Pick a style and a few setups that fit your time, money and temperament, go deep on them, judge them on a real sample of logged trades, and don't hop to a new setup after a short losing run.

facts.quote: Most individual investors do not have the wealth, the time, or the temperament to make money and to sustain the devastating losses that day trading can bring.
facts.claim: The SEC says most individual investors lack the wealth, the time or the temperament to make money day trading and survive its losses.

facts.quote: Day traders must watch the market continuously during the day at their computer terminals.
facts.claim: Day trading means watching the market all day long.

facts.quote: Day trading is an extremely stressful and expensive full-time job
facts.claim: The SEC calls day trading an extremely stressful, expensive full-time job.

facts.quote: Day traders typically suffer severe financial losses in their first months of trading, and many never graduate to profit-making status.
facts.claim: New day traders typically lose heavily in their first months, and many never become profitable.

facts.quote: day traders should only risk money they can afford to lose.
facts.claim: Only trade money you can afford to lose.

facts.quote: Don't believe advertising claims that promise quick and sure profits from day trading.
facts.claim: Don't believe ads that promise quick, sure day-trading profits.

facts.quote: Remember that "educational" seminars, classes, and books about day trading may not be objective
facts.claim: Day-trading seminars, classes and books may not be objective: the seller may profit if you start.

facts.quote: trading throughout the day is time-intensive and requires that you pay continuous attention to your holdings and the market as a whole.
facts.claim: FINRA says intraday trading takes a lot of time and continuous attention to your positions and the market.

facts.quote: Strategies that involve frequent trading on margin generally are not appropriate for investors with: limited financial resources; limited investment or trading experience; or low risk tolerance.
facts.claim: FINRA says frequent margin trading generally doesn't suit people with limited money, limited experience or low risk tolerance.

facts.quote: Given the significant risks, you should never fund this type of trading with essential assets.
facts.claim: Never fund frequent intraday trading with money you need.

facts.quote: Our job is to find the ways of trading that best play to our personality strengths.
facts.claim: Steenbarger: your job is to find the ways of trading that play to your personality's strengths.

facts.quote: A great way to see how your personality contributes to your trading success is to study your best trades and how you succeeded.
facts.claim: Study your best trades, and how you won them, to see what you do well.

facts.quote: Are you a generalist in your trading, trading multiple markets and strategies, or are you a specialist, who does one or two things really well?
facts.claim: Steenbarger describes a specialist as a trader who does one or two things really well.

facts.quote: we experience emotional disruptions in our trading, not because we lack discipline or are overcome with greed or frustration, but because we are trying to trade in a way that doesn't leverage who we actually are
facts.claim: Steenbarger: emotional upsets in trading often come from trading in a way that doesn't fit who you are, not only from weak discipline.

facts.quote: This fast trader excels in pattern recognition and also excels in the ability to maintain high levels of focus and flexibility of perception within and across trading days.
facts.claim: Steenbarger's fast, short-term trader is strong at pattern recognition and at holding focus for long stretches.

facts.quote: When the fast trader attempts to trade longer time frames, the near-term pattern recognition (a strength) can actually pose distractions.
facts.claim: A fast trader's quick pattern reading can become a distraction on longer time frames.

facts.quote: problems with our trading may not occur due to our weaknesses, but because of a misapplication of our strengths
facts.claim: Trading problems can come from using your strengths in the wrong place, not only from weaknesses.

facts.quote: Many, many times, traders do not live up to their potential simply because they are trading markets and methods that do not draw upon their strengths.
facts.claim: Traders often fall short because their markets and methods don't use their strengths.

facts.quote: Without that fit, they are not absorbed in what they do; frustration replaces focus and learning suffers.
facts.claim: Without fit, frustration replaces focus and learning suffers.

facts.quote: success will not be found in better indicators, improved self-help techniques, or any of the endless parade of chart patterns, wave formations, numerology schemes, or moving average arrays.
facts.claim: Steenbarger: success won't come from better indicators or another chart pattern; it comes from fit.

facts.quote: A niche is a domain of endeavor that not only captures our talents and skills, but also our deepest values and interests.
facts.claim: A niche is work that uses your talents and skills and also your deepest values and interests.

facts.quote: traders experience a high failure rate, not just because of the difficulty of the work, but because they place their capital at risk before they find a true niche within the trading world.
facts.claim: Steenbarger: many traders fail partly because they risk capital before they find their niche.

facts.quote: Trade in simulation mode before you put money at risk, trade one lots before you trade larger size. Make your mistakes when your exposure is lowest.
facts.claim: Practise in simulation, then at the smallest size, before you trade bigger.

facts.quote: Markets change, and their patterns change.  Few traders make as much in range bound markets and non-volatile markets as in trending, volatile ones.
facts.claim: Markets and their patterns change; most traders make less in quiet, range-bound markets than in trending ones.

facts.quote: It's the reworking of old trading processes and the addition of new ones that enable traders to stay profitable when markets go from trending and non-volatile to volatile and choppy.
facts.claim: When markets turn choppy, reworking old processes and adding new ones keeps traders profitable.

facts.quote: You cannot play to your strengths if you aren't intimately familiar with what those strengths are.  Working on correcting weaknesses only gets you so far.
facts.claim: Know your strengths well; fixing weaknesses only gets you so far.

facts.quote: Traders don't need education.  What traders most need is training.
facts.claim: Steenbarger: traders need training (learning by doing) more than more education.

facts.quote: Trading the wrong product, time frame, or trading style would be like asking NBA star Steph Curry (a great point guard) to play the center position.
facts.claim: Bellafiore: trading the wrong style or time frame is like making a great point guard play center.

facts.quote: Consider how you have been successful in the past and find setups that accentuate those strengths.
facts.claim: Bellafiore: look at how you've succeeded and pick setups that build on those strengths.

facts.quote: Tag and Measure your trades (keep score!)
facts.claim: Bellafiore: tag and measure your trades; keep score.

facts.quote: Increase risk on setups that measure well in real-time (sizing).
facts.claim: Bellafiore: size up on the setups that measure well in live trading.

facts.quote: Find a trading niche that has edge and leverages your personality and cognitive strengths.
facts.claim: Bellafiore: find a niche that has edge and plays to your personality and the way you think.

facts.quote: His ability to process information quickly is distinct.  Sticking to scalping, with now large size as he has grown as a trader, allows him to play to his strengths
facts.claim: SMB's scalper processes information fast, and sticking to scalping plays to that strength.

facts.quote: Frequent Flyer data dumped on our conference room table irrefutable evidence for a capital bump, in the way of his trading stats for this trade.
facts.claim: An SMB trader earned more buying power on his favourite setup by showing his stats for it.

facts.quote: Linda Raschke, trader and trading educator, stresses learning one setup well and then and only then moving to another.
facts.claim: Linda Raschke teaches learning one setup well before moving to another.

facts.quote: We expose new traders to the different trading strategies working for our top traders, let them experiment, and then choose the setups best for them.
facts.claim: SMB has new traders try several working strategies, then choose the setups that suit them.

facts.quote: I really like for the new trader to gain exposure to setups with edge, experimenting with them on a demo, finding your niche, and then building your PlayBook.
facts.claim: Bellafiore: try setups with edge on a demo, find your niche, then build your playbook.

facts.quote: Focus most of your energy trading, measuring and reviewing your PlayBook trades.  Leave some time to expand your PlayBook, with new trades.
facts.claim: Put most of your energy into your playbook trades, and leave some time to add new ones.

facts.quote: one of my worst trades is a second day play and it has a large tag count so it means I've taken it many times
facts.claim: An SMB trader's tags showed one of his worst setups was one he had taken many times.

facts.quote: the sample set is very big and that tells me that I shouldn't be taking that trade anymore
facts.claim: With a big sample of a losing setup, he decided to stop taking it.

facts.quote: There are hundreds, if not thousands, of trading systems that work, but after purchasing one, the typical trader will not follow it or trade it exactly as it was intended.
facts.claim: Tharp: many systems work, but the typical buyer doesn't trade one as intended.

facts.quote: Why not? Because the system didn't fit them and their style of trading.
facts.claim: Tharp: buyers don't follow working systems because the systems don't fit them.

facts.quote: if your trading system doesn't match your beliefs about the markets, you will eventually find a way to sabotage your trading.
facts.claim: A system that clashes with what you believe about markets is one you'll end up sabotaging.

facts.quote: Please note that you can only get a good idea of your system's expectancy when you have a minimum of thirty trades to analyze.
facts.claim: Tharp: you need at least thirty trades to get a good idea of a system's expectancy.

facts.quote: In order to really get a clear picture of the system's expectancy, you should actually have somewhere between 100 and 200.
facts.claim: Tharp: for a clear picture of expectancy, have 100 to 200 trades.

facts.quote: It's best to start small (very small) and minimize the "tuition paid" to learn the new strategy.
facts.claim: Start a new strategy very small so learning it costs little.

facts.quote: Once you've proven that you can consistently and profitably trade the strategy over a meaningful period of time (months, not days), you can begin to ramp up your position sizing strategies.
facts.claim: Size up only after months, not days, of consistent, profitable trading of that strategy.

facts.quote: Systems must be evaluated and revised to adapt to changing market conditions.
facts.claim: Systems need checking and revising as markets change.

facts.quote: Expectancy is simply the mean, or average, R-multiple generated.
facts.claim: Expectancy is the average R per trade.

facts.quote: despite the fact that only one of your trades was a winner and 99% of your trades were losers.
facts.claim: Tharp's example makes money even though 99% of its trades lose: the one winner is big.

facts.quote: after a losing streak, the next bet has a better chance of being a winner. If that's your belief, you'll be tempted to increase your position size when you shouldn't.
facts.claim: Believing a win is due after a losing streak (the gambler's fallacy) tempts you to size up when you shouldn't.

facts.quote: When traders take the time to write down all their beliefs (about themselves, the markets, money, etc.), then they can establish a much better idea of what they want to trade, how they want to trade
facts.claim: Writing down your beliefs about yourself and markets clarifies what and how you want to trade.

facts.quote: Many professional traders have multiple systems that operate in multiple time frames over many markets
facts.claim: Tharp notes many professionals run several systems across time frames and markets.

facts.quote: Smaller sample sizes have more volatile and less reliable statistical results.
facts.claim: Small samples give jumpy, unreliable results.

facts.quote: When a sample size is too small, accurate and trustworthy conclusions cannot be drawn.
facts.claim: From too small a sample you can't draw a trustworthy conclusion.

facts.quote: once a trader has confidence in their trading plan, they must have the discipline to stay the course, even when there are the inevitable losing streaks.
facts.claim: Losing streaks are inevitable; a plan you trust needs the discipline to stay the course through them.

facts.quote: Learn what you can from others, then back off and establish your own market identity, based on your unique skills and risk tolerance.
facts.claim: Learn from others, then build your own trading identity on your skills and risk tolerance.

facts.quote: It's natural for traders to emulate their financial heroes, but it's also a perfect way to lose money.
facts.claim: Copying your trading heroes is a good way to lose money.

facts.quote: Many traders can profit in certain markets like a strong uptrend, but they fail over time because their strategies don't adapt to changing conditions.
facts.claim: Strategies that don't adapt to changing markets fail over time.

facts.quote: Some traders try to make up for insufficient skills with expensive software
facts.claim: Expensive software doesn't make up for weak skills.

facts.quote: Compound probability is equal to the probability of the first event multiplied by the probability of the second event.
facts.claim: The chance of two independent events both happening is their two chances multiplied.

facts.quote: If the probability of getting heads is 50 percent, then the chances of getting heads twice in a row would be (.50 X .50), or .25 (25 percent).
facts.claim: Two heads in a row at 50% each is 0.50 x 0.50 = 25%.

facts.quote: The time commitment for swing trading isn't as intensive as day trading, since positions are held for a few days to several weeks.
facts.claim: Swing trading takes less time than day trading because positions are held for days to weeks.

facts.quote: While offering flexibility, swing trading carries the risk of overnight and weekend market exposures.
facts.claim: Swing trading is flexible but carries overnight and weekend risk.

facts.quote: Losing streaks can happen to the best of us, but sometimes a bout of bad luck can actually reflect a problem with our trading strategy.
facts.claim: Losing streaks happen to good traders, but sometimes one points to a real problem with the strategy.

facts.quote: To begin, traders should look at whether they're losing or making money on a net basis, then look for patterns in their wins and losses.
facts.claim: After a streak, check whether you're net up or down, then look for patterns in your wins and losses.

facts.quote: As a trader works to figure out what needs fixing, there's no harm in reducing the size of your trades.
facts.claim: While you work out what needs fixing, trading smaller does no harm.

facts.quote: One of the biggest secrets of successful trading is finding a trading system that fits you personally.
facts.claim: Tharp: finding a trading system that fits you personally is one of the biggest secrets of successful trading.

facts.quote: if winning trades employ fundamental analysis and losing trades are based on technical analysis, a trader might want to focus more on fundamentals for a while.
facts.claim: Schwab: if your winners come from one approach and your losers from another, lean on the one that wins for a while.

facts.quote: They should never use money they will need for daily living expenses, retirement, take out a second mortgage, or use their student loan money for day trading.
facts.claim: Never day trade with money you need to live on, retirement money, a second mortgage or student loans.

facts.quote: I've been taking second day trades for about a year now and I've tried to work on them
facts.claim: Before he stopped, the SMB trader had taken that setup for about a year and tried to fix it.

facts.quote: No losing-streak rule: size is cut only by the drawdown ladder, in percent (A8, B13, B14).
facts.claim: Our rule B17: there is no losing-streak size cut; only the drawdown ladder, in percent, cuts size.

facts.quote: New traders start at 0.25% risk per trade until 50 journaled trades followed the rules, then size up.
facts.claim: Our rule C37: new traders risk 0.25% a trade until 50 journaled trades followed the rules.

facts.quote: Never raise risk past the rules after a run of winners.
facts.claim: Our rule D45: never raise risk past the rules after a run of winners.

facts.quote: We swing trade: days to a few weeks; a winner can be held longer while it keeps working.
facts.claim: Our rule C35: we swing trade, holding days to a few weeks, longer while a winner keeps working.

facts.quote: A drawdown is how far the account is below its highest value, open trades included, checked at least weekly.
facts.claim: Our rule A8: a drawdown is how far the account sits below its peak; the ladder cuts size by it.

facts.quote: Each month, review the numbers: win rate, average win and loss in R, expectancy, and other statistics.
facts.claim: Our rule E59: each month, review win rate, average win and loss in R, and expectancy.

walkthroughs.title: Fit comes first
steps: Every style asks something of you. Day trading wants your eyes on the market all day.
The SEC says most investors lack the wealth, the time or the temperament for it. Swing trading takes far less screen time.
Plenty of traders fall short just because their method doesn't play to their strengths.
So pick the style that fits your clock, your money and your nerves. For us, that's swing trading.

walkthroughs.title: Go deep on a few
steps: Coaches split on how to start. Linda Raschke says learn one setup well first. SMB has you sample a few with edge.
You end up with a short playbook that suits you. A specialist does one or two things really well.
Most of your energy goes into trading, logging and reviewing those. Test new ideas on the side, very small.

walkthroughs.title: Write your lane down
steps: Write it down: your style, the few setups you'll trade, and why they fit you.
Tag every trade by setup and keep score. That's how you find out what you actually trade well.
Don't grade a setup off a few trades. Van Tharp wanted thirty at least, and 100 to 200 for a clear picture.
Starting out, risk 0.25% a trade until you've logged 50 trades that followed the rules. Then size up.

questions.q: Tap the word the SEC used.
questions.sentence: Most investors lack the wealth, the time or the ___ to make money day trading, the SEC warns.
questions.why: Temperament. The SEC's page on day trading names three things most individual investors lack. They are the wealth, the time and the temperament to make money at it and survive its losses. The warning is about day trading, so weigh it when you pick that lane.
questions.lesson_line: Pick a style that fits your money, your hours and your nerves.
questions.simple: Temperament, because the SEC says most investors lack the wealth, the time or the temperament to make money day trading.

reasons: one cited fact only (f1)
simple and why trimmed in wave9 to what f1 says

questions.q: Steenbarger's view: when trading keeps upsetting you, the cause is a style that doesn't fit you, not weak discipline.
questions.why: He's right, and it's worth sitting with. Steenbarger says the upsets don't come from a lack of discipline. They come from trading in a way that doesn't fit who you are. Without that fit, frustration replaces focus and learning suffers. Tharp says the same about beliefs. Trade a system that clashes with what you believe about markets and you'll find a way to sabotage it. So if every trade feels like a fight, don't just grind harder. Check the fit first. Willpower won't hold a style you don't believe in for long.
questions.lesson_line: If every trade feels like a fight, check the fit before you blame your willpower.
questions.simple: True. Steenbarger says the upsets come from a style that doesn't fit you, not from weak discipline.

reasons: statement reworded in wave9 so True is not the only hedged statement in the lesson

questions.q: You work full time and get a lunch break to check prices. That's enough screen time to day trade.
questions.why: No, not even close. Day trading wants your eyes on the market all day. FINRA says it's time-intensive and needs continuous attention to your holdings and the market. The SEC calls it an extremely stressful, expensive full-time job. You already have one of those. A look at lunch leaves your positions unwatched for the rest of the session. With a day job, you swing trade. That's our lane. Do the work at night, set your alerts and your stop, and let the trade work while you're at your desk.
questions.lesson_line: Day trading takes the whole session. A lunch break isn't screen time.
questions.simple: False. Day trading needs your eyes on the market all day, and a lunch break isn't that.

questions.q: Mike Bellafiore of SMB Capital tells new traders to find their niche. What is he telling you to find?
choices: Edge that fits your strengths
The best win-rate setup
What top traders use
A corner of obscure stocks
questions.why: Edge that fits your strengths. Two halves, and you need both. Bellafiore's line is a niche that has edge and plays to your personality and the way you think. Edge means the setup makes money over a real sample of your own trades. Fit means you'll actually take it the way it's meant to be taken. A setup that pays but fights your nature gets skipped, rushed or second-guessed. A setup you love with no edge just loses slowly. So check your log for the edge, and be honest with yourself about the fit. I want both before I put real size on anything.
questions.lesson_line: Your niche is where real edge meets the way you think.

wrong.The best win-rate setup: Win rate isn't edge. Tharp's example makes money with 99% of its trades losing, because the one winner is big. And a high win rate does nothing for you if the setup doesn't suit you.
wrong.What top traders use: Their lane fits them, not you. Investopedia's list of trading rules calls copying your heroes a perfect way to lose money.
wrong.A corner of obscure stocks: Not what he means. A niche here is a way of trading, with edge, that plays to how you think. It isn't a quiet corner of the market.

questions.simple: Edge that fits your strengths. You need a setup that makes money and a style you'll actually follow.

deeper.trap: Win rate is not edge. Van Tharp's example makes money even though 99% of its trades lose, because the one winner is big. So a niche is not 'the setup that wins most often'. And copying what top traders use skips the fit half: Investopedia's rules call emulating your heroes a perfect way to lose money. Look for edge you can prove and a style you will actually follow.

reasons: re-asked in wave9 as Bellafiore's definition: Steenbarger's niche (f23) has no edge in it

questions.q: Tap the word that completes the advice.
questions.sentence: To find your strengths, Steenbarger says study your ___ trades.
questions.why: Best. Steenbarger says study your best trades, and how you succeeded, to see how your personality helps you win. Bellafiore says look at how you've succeeded and pick setups that build on those strengths. Schwab adds that if your winners come from one approach, lean on it for a while. This does not mean skip your losers. Schwab says look for patterns in both your wins and your losses.
questions.lesson_line: Your winners show you your lane. Study them as hard as your losers.
questions.simple: Best, because your winning trades show what you do well, and that points you to the setups that fit you.

reasons: fixed before (checker 2026-11-09)

questions.q: You've decided to specialize. So from now on you trade one setup and never add another.
questions.why: Too far. Specializing means going deep, not freezing your list. Steenbarger's specialist does one or two things really well. That's the model: a few setups you know cold. Most of your energy goes into trading, measuring and reviewing those. But markets change, and a lane that never adds anything gets stuck when they do. Steenbarger says reworking old processes and adding new ones keeps traders profitable when markets turn choppy. So leave some time for new ideas, and test them small, on the side. Plenty of pros run more than one system anyway.
questions.lesson_line: Go deep on a few setups. Add new ones slowly, on the side.
questions.simple: False. Specializing means going deep on a few setups, and you still make some time to add new ones.

questions.q: Tharp says hundreds of trading systems work. Yet the typical trader who buys one still fails with it. Why?
choices: It doesn't fit, so it isn't followed
The seller hid some of the real rules
Markets change too fast for systems
They traded it far too small
questions.answer: It doesn't fit, so it isn't followed
questions.why: It doesn't fit him, so he doesn't follow it. Tharp says hundreds, if not thousands, of systems work. But after buying one, the typical trader won't trade it exactly as it was intended. His reason: the system didn't fit them and their style of trading. Steenbarger sees the same thing. Traders fall short when their methods don't draw on their strengths. A good system you won't follow is worth nothing to you. That's why fit gets checked before you spend a dollar or risk one.
questions.lesson_line: A system you won't follow is worth nothing to you. Fit comes first.

wrong.The seller hid some of the real rules: Tharp doesn't blame the seller. Hundreds, if not thousands, of systems work. The problem is the fit with the trader.
wrong.Markets change too fast for systems: Systems do need revising as markets change. That's not the reason Tharp gives here, though. Buyers don't follow what they bought.
wrong.They traded it far too small: Small is how Tharp says to start a new strategy. Size can't fix a system you won't follow.

questions.simple: It doesn't fit the buyer, so he doesn't trade it the way it was meant to be traded.

reasons: fixed before (checker 2026-11-10)

questions.q: Steenbarger says the work is hard, but that's not the only reason new traders fail. They risk real money before finding what?
choices: Their true niche
The right software
Enough trading books
A strong bull market
questions.why: Their true niche. Steenbarger says the failure rate is high not just because the work is hard. Traders put capital at risk before they find a true niche. That's paying full price for lessons you could have had cheap. Do it in order. Bellafiore has new traders try setups with edge on a demo, find their niche, then build a playbook. Steenbarger says trade in simulation, then at the smallest size, before you go bigger. Make your mistakes when your exposure is lowest.
questions.lesson_line: Find your lane on paper and at small size first. Then put real money behind it.

wrong.The right software: Software can't cover weak skills. Steenbarger says success won't come from better indicators or another chart pattern.
wrong.Enough trading books: Reading isn't the gap. Steenbarger says traders need training, learning by doing, more than education.
wrong.A strong bull market: He isn't talking about timing the market. He means finding the trading that fits your talents, skills and interests.

questions.simple: Their true niche. Too many traders risk real money before they find the kind of trading that fits them.

reasons: key text lengthened in wave9 to balance the choices (was 11 characters against 18 to 20)

questions.story: You love fast trades and quick calls. You work 9 to 5 with no screen during market hours. Your evenings are free.
questions.q: What lane do you pick for now?
choices: Swing trades planned at night
Day trade the open at work
Quit your job to day trade
Whatever worked last month
questions.why: Swing trades planned at night. Your hours make this call before your taste does. FINRA says intraday trading needs continuous attention, and you can't give that from your desk at work. Swing trades are held for a few days to several weeks, so they need far less screen time. Do your scans in the evening. Mark the trigger and the stop, set your alerts, and let it work. The trade-off is overnight and weekend risk. That's the price of not watching. Fast trades can wait until you have the screen time.
questions.lesson_line: Your schedule picks the lane before your taste does.

wrong.Day trade the open at work: The open needs your full attention, and you're at work then. FINRA says intraday trading needs continuous attention.
wrong.Quit your job to day trade: Don't bet your living on it. The SEC says new day traders typically suffer severe losses in their first months. Never day trade with money you need to live on.
wrong.Whatever worked last month: Last month's hot thing says nothing about your hours. Start from your schedule.

questions.simple: Swing trades planned at night. You can't watch the market at work, and swing trades need far less screen time.

reasons: fixed before (checker 2026-11-09)

questions.story: Sam can watch the market all day. He reads charts fast, loves quick decisions and stays sharp for hours. Waiting days for a trade bores him.
questions.q: Which lane would you point Sam toward?
choices: Short-term day trades
Multi-week position trades
Long-term buy and hold
Whatever his mentor trades
questions.why: Short-term day trades. Everything about Sam says speed. Steenbarger's fast trader excels at pattern recognition and holds his focus within and across trading days. That's Sam. SMB has a scalper who processes information fast, and sticking to scalping plays to that strength. Sam also has the hours, and day trading needs eyes on the market all day. Fit isn't the whole check, though. The SEC says most investors lack the wealth, the time or the temperament for day trading. So Sam checks his money too. We swing trade ourselves, days to a few weeks. This one's about Sam's fit, not ours.
questions.lesson_line: Match the clock to the person. Then check that the money can carry it.

wrong.Multi-week position trades: Long holds sit on his speed instead of using it. Steenbarger says find the ways of trading that play to your strengths.
wrong.Long-term buy and hold: That asks Sam to sit still for years. It throws away the speed he's good at.
wrong.Whatever his mentor trades: His mentor's lane fits his mentor. Learn from others, then build your own trading identity.

questions.simple: Short-term day trades. Sam reads charts fast, stays sharp for hours and can watch the market all day.

questions.story: Over 200 logged trades, a pattern shows. Your multi-day swings on strong themes make money. Your quick scalps at the open lose it.
questions.q: What's your next move?
choices: Narrow to the multi-day swings
Drill scalps until they work
Split time evenly between both
Add a third style to compare
questions.why: Narrow to the multi-day swings. Over 200 trades, your record shows where you are strong. Schwab says first check whether you're net up or down, then look for patterns in your wins and losses. Steenbarger says study your best trades, and fixing weaknesses only gets you so far. Bellafiore says pick setups that build on how you've succeeded. Narrowing is not a ban on new ideas. Leave a little time to test new trades.
questions.lesson_line: Let your own record pick the lane. Then put most of your energy there.

wrong.Drill scalps until they work: Fixing weaknesses only gets you so far, Steenbarger says. Your record already shows a strength to build on.
wrong.Split time evenly between both: Half your energy would go to what your record says you do worst. Most of it belongs on what works.
wrong.Add a third style to compare: More styles spread you thinner. Your 200 trades already point to a lane.

questions.simple: Narrow to the swings, because 200 trades show that is where you win, and your strengths deserve most of your energy.

reasons: fixed before (checker 2026-11-09)

questions.q: A setup wins 40% of trades. Treat trades as independent. What's the chance the next six all lose? Nearest whole percent.
questions.why: 5%. Each trade loses 60% of the time, so six losses in a row is 0.6 multiplied by itself six times. Unlikely in any one stretch, but you'll trade many stretches.
questions.lesson_line: Losing streaks come with any edge. Expect them before they show up.

questions.q: Over 150 logged breakout trades, 40% won, averaging 2.5R. The losers lost 1R on average. What's the average R per trade?
questions.why: 0.4R. Expectancy is the average R per trade: 40% of trades make 2.5R and 60% lose 1R. You lose more trades than you win and still average 0.4R a trade.
questions.lesson_line: Judge a setup by its average R over many trades, not by its win rate or its last streak.

questions.story: Your new breakout setup tested well on past charts. Live, you've taken six trades by the plan. All six lost.
questions.q: Now what?
choices: Review them and keep logging
Drop it and start a new setup
Double size to win it back
Keep going and skip the review
questions.why: Review the six and keep logging. Six trades tells you almost nothing yet. Tharp says you need a minimum of thirty to get a good idea of a system's expectancy. Small samples swing all over the place. But don't skip the review either. Schwab says a streak can sometimes point to a real problem with the strategy. So pull up all six. Check that each one triggered the way the plan says, and that the stops sat where they belonged. If the trades were clean, keep taking it by the plan and keep logging. And never size up to win it back. A win is never due.
questions.lesson_line: Six trades is a streak, not a verdict. Review them, then log more before you judge.

wrong.Drop it and start a new setup: Six trades is too few to judge. Hop now and you start from zero with another tiny sample.
wrong.Double size to win it back: That's the gambler's fallacy. Thinking a win is due after a streak tempts you to size up right when you shouldn't.
wrong.Keep going and skip the review: Streaks happen to good traders, but sometimes one points to a real flaw. Look at the six first.

questions.simple: Review the six and keep logging. Six trades is too few to judge, but a streak can still hide a real flaw.

deeper.trap: Two opposite mistakes start from the same six losses. One reads the streak as proof and drops the setup, but six trades is far below Tharp's minimum of thirty. The other believes a win is now due and sizes up, which is the gambler's fallacy Tharp warns about. Both react to the streak instead of the sample. Look at the six trades for a real flaw, and keep logging.

reasons: cold check 2026-11-12: B17 size lines (f74, f78) dropped; 'a losing run cuts size only through drawdown' overreached against B16 (monthly loss limit) and A1 (recent results pick risk), and no choice is about cutting size
Schwab s19 and Investopedia s15 unreachable 2026-11-12; f56, f57, f67, f68 rest on the 2026-11-09 read

questions.q: You've been trading a new setup small, and it's working. When does it earn a bigger size from you?
choices: After your logged trades prove it
After two or three big wins
When you feel sure about it
When a mentor swears by it
questions.answer: After your logged trades prove it
questions.why: When your logged trades prove it. Two or three wins feels like proof, but it's a tiny sample, and small samples can fool you. We put hard lines on this. A new trader risks 0.25% a trade until 50 journaled trades followed the rules. And we never raise risk past the rules after a run of winners. Tharp's bar is months of consistent, profitable trading on that strategy, not days. Bellafiore says increase risk on the setups that measure well in real time. So keep tagging every trade, and let that setup's numbers earn the bigger size. Not the mood.
questions.lesson_line: Size follows proof. Your own logged numbers earn the bigger size, inside our rules.

wrong.After two or three big wins: Two or three trades is a tiny sample, and small samples give unreliable results. We never raise risk past the rules after a run of winners.
wrong.When you feel sure about it: A feeling isn't a record. An SMB trader got more buying power by putting his stats on the table, not his confidence.
wrong.When a mentor swears by it: His record isn't yours. Learn from others, then build your own trading identity on your skills and risk tolerance.

questions.simple: When your own logged trades prove it. A few wins or a good feeling is too small a sample to size up on.

reasons: re-taught in wave9 with our rules C37 and D45
size by setup grade (D38, E49) is not taught here; flagged for the owner

questions.story: A year of trades, each tagged by setup. Setup A: 120 trades, net down every quarter. Setup B: 150 trades, steady gains.
questions.q: What's your record telling you to do?
choices: Drop A and focus on B
Keep both, A will turn
Trade setup A bigger
Add a third setup, C
questions.answer: Drop A and focus on B
questions.why: Drop A and put your energy into B. A has 120 trades and lost money every quarter. That's not a bad stretch, that's an answer. Tharp puts a clear picture of expectancy at 100 to 200 trades. A sits inside that range and loses in every part of it. A trader on SMB's desk made this same call. He'd worked on his worst setup for about a year, and the big sample told him to stop. B has 150 trades of steady gains. Bellafiore says increase risk on setups that measure well, and B does. This is why you tag every trade by setup. Without the tags, A hides inside B's gains.
questions.lesson_line: A small sample can fool you. A big one deserves a hearing.

wrong.Keep both, A will turn: Hope isn't a sample. A has 120 trades and lost in every quarter. Tharp puts a clear picture at 100 to 200 trades.
wrong.Trade setup A bigger: Backwards. Bellafiore says increase risk on setups that measure well in real time. A has measured badly for 120 trades.
wrong.Add a third setup, C: You already have a setup that works. Put most of your energy into B before you add anything.

questions.simple: Drop A and focus on B. A lost every quarter over 120 trades, a big enough sample to trust.

deeper.trap: A big sample is not the same as a long streak. Setup A lost money over 120 trades and in every quarter. The result does not hang on one bad stretch. Tharp's minimum for a good read is thirty trades, and his clear picture needs 100 to 200. Before you drop a setup, ask how many trades it has and how many different stretches of the market they cover.

reasons: fixed before (checker 2026-11-09)
choices rebalanced in wave9 (the key was 12 characters against 15 to 22)

questions.story: Your pullback setup is solidly positive over 150 logged trades. A friend's new setup made him 30% last month. You're tempted to switch.
questions.q: What's the play?
choices: Paper trade his on the side
Switch to his setup this week
Run both at full size now
Never look at a new setup
questions.answer: Paper trade his on the side
questions.why: Paper trade his on the side. His 30% is one month from one trader. Small samples give jumpy, unreliable results, and that's about as small as it gets. Your pullback setup has 150 logged trades behind it. Don't trade that proof for somebody's hot month. Keep most of your energy on the setup that's paying you, and leave a little time for new ones. Tharp says start any new strategy very small. If his earns a place over time, it joins your lane. If it doesn't, it cost you nothing.
questions.lesson_line: Keep your lane. Test new ideas on the side, small, until they earn a place.

wrong.Switch to his setup this week: You'd swap 150 trades of your own proof for one month of his. Small samples give unreliable results.
wrong.Run both at full size now: Tharp says start a new strategy very small, so learning it costs little. Full size on day one pays full tuition.
wrong.Never look at a new setup: Too rigid. Bellafiore leaves time to add new trades, and Steenbarger says adding new processes keeps traders profitable as markets change.

questions.simple: Paper trade his on the side. One month of his results is a tiny sample, and your 150 trades back yours.

deeper.trap: The trap is the size of his number. A 30% month looks like proof, but it is one month from one trader. Small samples give jumpy, unreliable results. Your 150 trades say far more about your own edge than his month does. Learn what you can from him, then keep building your own trading identity on your own skills.

reasons: fixed before (checker 2026-11-11)

questions.q: Steenbarger says a fast trader's quick pattern reading, a real strength, can become a distraction once he holds for weeks.
questions.why: That's right, and it catches people off guard. Steenbarger says when a fast trader tries longer time frames, the near-term pattern reading can actually pose distractions. The thing that makes him good on fast trades gets in his way. He sees every wiggle on a trade that's meant to run for weeks. Steenbarger's point is bigger than one trader. Trading problems can come from misapplying your strengths, not just from your weaknesses. Bellafiore compares the wrong style to asking a great point guard to play center. A fast trader can still hold longer. He just has to know where his strength works.
questions.lesson_line: A strength in one style can trip you up in another. Trade where your strength fits.
questions.simple: True. Quick pattern reading helps on fast trades but can distract you on trades held for weeks.

deeper.trap: The trap is thinking a strength works everywhere. Steenbarger says problems can come from a misapplication of our strengths, not just our weaknesses. A fast trader's eye for near-term patterns is his example: a gift on short trades, a possible distraction on long ones. So match the time frame to the skill, then judge the match on your own logged trades.

reasons: rests on two linked publishers only (Steenbarger and Bellafiore, see conflicts); the pattern-reading claim itself is Steenbarger's, so the statement now names him
flipped to a True statement in wave9 to balance True and False and break the absolute-means-False pattern
final check: why and deeper kept to f18's 'can'

questions.story: Your breakout setup paid for two years. The market turned choppy, and over the last 60 trades it has lost steadily, rules followed.
questions.q: How do you handle it?
choices: Study what changed and adapt it
Keep trading it and wait it out
Jump to whatever's working now
Drop it, 60 trades is enough proof
questions.answer: Study what changed and adapt it
questions.why: Study what changed and adapt it. Sixty trades is a real sample, but look where they came from. Every one came after the market turned choppy, on a setup with two good years behind it. Tharp says systems must be evaluated and revised as markets change. Steenbarger says reworking old processes is what keeps traders profitable when markets go choppy. Pull up the losers and lay them next to the good years. See if the bases got sloppier or the breakouts started failing more. Then adjust what you take, or wait for the market that suits it. Waiting blind and hopping both skip that work.
questions.lesson_line: A lane can drift with the market. Study it, adapt it, and don't hop.

wrong.Jump to whatever's working now: That's setup hopping. You'd give up two years of knowing this setup for one you have no record with.
wrong.Keep trading it and wait it out: Strategies that don't adapt to changing markets fail over time. Waiting without studying it makes the lesson expensive.
wrong.Drop it, 60 trades is enough proof: Sixty trades clears Tharp's minimum of thirty, but they all come from one choppy stretch. Study the change before you scrap two good years.

questions.simple: Study what changed and adapt it. A setup that paid for two years is facing a new market, not proven broken.

deeper.trap: Two cases look alike and are not. A setup that loses over a big sample across many kinds of market has shown no edge, so you drop it. A setup that paid for two years and then loses in one choppy stretch may be out of season. Steenbarger notes few traders make as much in range-bound markets as in trending ones. Study what changed and rework the setup before you decide.

reasons: re-keyed in wave9 off Schwab's 'trade smaller' f69
final check: size lines (B17, A8) dropped because our market reading (F65) also guides size in a choppy market and this lesson does not teach it
fixed before (checker 2026-11-09)

questions.story: You're new, with a full-time job and $8,000 you can't afford to lose. A course says day trading is the fastest way to get rich.
questions.q: What's the honest call?
choices: Pass, it fits neither time nor money
Sign up and day trade the $8,000
Buy the course to learn first
Day trade on margin to grow it faster
questions.answer: Pass, it fits neither time nor money
questions.why: Pass. It fits neither your hours nor your money. You've got a full-time job, and the SEC calls day trading an extremely stressful, expensive full-time job of its own. The SEC also says only risk money you can afford to lose. This $8,000 isn't that. Now look at who's pitching. The SEC warns day-trading courses may not be objective, and says don't believe ads promising quick, sure profits. Anyone selling speed is selling to your goal, not your limits. Start where you are. Learn to swing trade, plan at night, and only risk money you can afford to lose.
questions.lesson_line: Pick a lane your money and your hours can survive. Ignore anyone selling speed.

wrong.Sign up and day trade the $8,000: That's money you can't afford to lose. The SEC says new day traders typically suffer severe losses in their first months.
wrong.Day trade on margin to grow it faster: Borrowing adds risk. FINRA says frequent margin trading generally doesn't suit people with limited money or experience. Never fund it with money you need.
wrong.Buy the course to learn first: The course sells day trading as the fastest way to get rich. The SEC says courses like that may not be objective. And it doesn't change your hours or your money.

questions.simple: Pass. Day trading is a full-time job, and the $8,000 is money you can't afford to lose.

deeper.trap: The pitch works because it names your goal, not your limits. Check three things before any lane: your hours, your money and your nerves. Here the hours and the money both fail. FINRA adds that frequent trading on margin generally doesn't suit people with limited money or experience. It says never fund that kind of trading with money you need.

reasons: fixed before (checker 2026-11-09)
a choice replaced again in wave9: 'Buy the course, then day trade later' still day traded, so the key was the only non-day-trade choice

questions.q: You buy a breakout the way we trade it. How long do you expect to hold it?
choices: Days to a few weeks
Minutes, flat by lunch
Hours, out by the close
Years, buy and hold
questions.why: Days to a few weeks. We swing trade. A winner can stay on longer while it keeps working, and a loser is gone at the stop. Swing trading takes less screen time than day trading, since positions are held for a few days to several weeks. That's why it fits around a job. You do the planning at night, and you're not glued to every tick. Day trading needs continuous attention all day. That's a different lane.
questions.simple: Days to a few weeks. We swing trade, and a winner can stay on longer while it keeps working.
questions.lesson_line: We swing trade: days to a few weeks, longer while a winner keeps working.

wrong.Minutes, flat by lunch: That's scalping, not our lane. We swing trade and hold for days to a few weeks.
wrong.Hours, out by the close: That's day trading. FINRA says it needs continuous attention all day. We hold for days to a few weeks.
wrong.Years, buy and hold: That's investing, not our lane. We hold days to a few weeks, longer only while a winner keeps working.

reasons: a rule from the owner's rulebook (C35)
new in wave9: the lesson leaned on C35 (q09, q10) without teaching it

questions.story: You tag every trade by setup in your journal. A new month just started.
questions.q: What do you do with last month's numbers?
choices: Review win rate, R and expectancy
Wait for a losing streak
Check only if you're down
Review only the losing trades
questions.answer: Review win rate, R and expectancy
questions.why: Review win rate, R and expectancy. We do this every month, up month or down. R is the amount you risked on a trade, and every win and loss gets measured in it. Expectancy is the average R per trade. That's the number that tells you whether a setup is paying you. Go setup by setup, using your tags, so you see which ones carry you and which ones bleed. Look at the winners as hard as the losers, since patterns show up in both. Skip the review and you find the bad setup the expensive way.
questions.simple: Review win rate, R and expectancy. We go over the numbers every month, setup by setup, up or down.
questions.lesson_line: Every month, run the numbers by setup: win rate, average win and loss in R, expectancy.

wrong.Wait for a losing streak: We review every month, streak or not. Wait for a streak and you've already paid for the lesson.
wrong.Check only if you're down: We review every month, up or down. Bellafiore says size up on setups that measure well, so the winners need measuring too.
wrong.Review only the losing trades: That's half the picture. Steenbarger says study your best trades to see what you do well.

reasons: a rule from the owner's rulebook (E59)
new in wave9: replaces cut q11 in the Practise rungs
Schwab s19 unreachable 2026-11-12; f68 rests on the 2026-11-09 read

questions.q: You want to find the setups that fit you. You open your journal. Which trades do you study first?
choices: Your best trades, and how you won them
Your worst trades, and how you lost them
Your newest trades, win or lose
Trades you skipped, to see the misses
questions.answer: Your best trades, and how you won them
questions.why: Your best trades, and how you won them. That's where you see what you actually do well. Pull up your top winners and look at what they share: the setup, the hold, how you got in. Bellafiore says look at how you've succeeded and pick setups that build on those strengths. If your winners keep coming from one approach and your losers from another, lean on the one that wins for a while. Schwab makes that same point. Review the losers too, since patterns show up in both. But you build your lane on what you already do well.
questions.lesson_line: Your winners show you your lane. Study them as hard as your losers.

wrong.Trades you skipped, to see the misses: Skipped trades aren't your trades. Your own winners show what you do well.
wrong.Your worst trades, and how you lost them: Worth reviewing, but losses mostly show what went wrong. Your strengths show up in your best trades.
wrong.Your newest trades, win or lose: Recent trades are just one slice. You want the ones that show what you do well.

questions.simple: Your best trades. How you won them shows what you do well, and which setups fit you.

reasons: Steenbarger, Bellafiore and Schwab agree

conflicts: One setup or a few: Steenbarger's specialist 'does one or two things really well' and Bellafiore keeps most energy on the playbook while leaving time to add trades; Van Tharp writes that many professionals run multiple systems across time frames and markets (f55). The unit teaches 'a few setups, deep' and never 'one setup forever' (q06 is keyed False on exactly that).

How a beginner starts: Bellafiore reports that Linda Raschke teaches one setup well before the next, while SMB has new traders sample several setups with edge (a week each, on a demo) and then choose. He says 'I am not suggesting we have the right answer here.' Shown as a difference between coaches in w2; never asked as a fact.

Publisher independence: Steenbarger (TraderFeed) and Bellafiore (SMB) are different publishers, but linked: SMB's techniques appear in Steenbarger's The Daily Trading Coach and Bellafiore's posts credit him. Keys that rest on both also cite Tharp, Investopedia, Schwab or a Tier 1 page wherever such a page says the same thing (q04, q06, q07, q02, q11, q08). q05 (study your best trades) now also cites Schwab (f71). Two keys rest on the two of them plus no third publisher: q10 (a fast thinker fits fast trades) and q18 (fast pattern reading does not carry over to week-long holds).

The SEC alert 'Day Trading: Your Dollars at Risk' dates from April 2005. Its lines on time, temperament and affording losses match FINRA's current page (June 04, 2026); its lines on commissions and firm costs are dated and are not used.

Van Tharp's 'a minimum of thirty trades' and '100 to 200' are his rule of thumb for judging expectancy (one publisher). They appear only in why / walk-through text, attributed to him; no question is keyed on either number.
The SMB trader in s13 is quoted from a video transcript (spoken words, no punctuation); only his own account is used, as his.
q12 assumes independent trades, as the question says. Real trades can cluster with market conditions, which makes long losing runs more likely, not less; no number in the file depends on that.

Track audit 2026-11-09: q12 and q13 are cut as duplicates of F9.03 q18 and q19 (the six-loss streak calc and the 40% / 2.5R expectancy calc), and q03 is kept over F11.01 q06. The note above about q12's independence assumption stays as the record.
